list.listitem: Clinical criteria for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) include new lung infiltrate in a ventilated patient and at least two of the following: temperature >38°C, leukopenia or leukocytosis, and purulent secretions. C Semi-quantitative culture is useful for the identifying causative organism; sampling by endotrachial aspiration is recommended for patients with VAP and using spontaneous sputum, induced sputum, or nasotracheal suctioning in non-ventilated patients with HAP. C

Antimicrobial therapy should be started promptly and based on local resistance patterns. The decision regarding single, dual or triple antibiotic therapy depends on patient mortality risk, risk factors for MDR pathogens, and whether HAP or VAP is treated.B
The recommended duration is 7 days for patients with HAP or VAP who have a good clinical response.B

Measures to prevent VAP include a bundle of services: oral decontamination with daily toothbrushing, elevating head of bed to 30° to 45°, use of a new ventilator circuit for each patient and replacing it when soiled, suction of subglottic secretion, and minimizing the duration of intubation. Inhaled aminoglycosides are also effective.A

background.definition: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is pneumonia that occur 48 to 72 hours after endotracheal intubation. Early onset VAP occur within 4 days of intubation, while late onset VAP occur 5 days or more after intubation. Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is pneumonia that begins after hospitalization but is not associated with mechanical ventilation.Nosocomial pneumonia encompasses both HAP and VAP.

list.listitem: VAP occurs in 8% to 28% of intubated patients.
The incidence is 1 to 4 per 1000 ventilator days.
VAP is the most common nosocomial infection in the ICU.
HAP and VAP, together, account for 21.8% of healthcare-associated infections, with 39.1% of those associated with a mechanical ventilator.
VAP has been shown to be associated with longer ICU and hospital lengths of stay.
VAP is caused by a wide spectrum of organisms.
The most common organisms causing nosocomial pneumonia are KEEPS: klebsiella, enterobacter, e.coli, pseudomonas aeurignosa, and staphylococcus aureus.
Common bacteria include aerobic Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter species.
Infections due to Gram-postive cocci such as Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA are increasing.
Most cases of VAP are caused by the aspiration of infected secretion from oropharynx, although a few cases occur secondary to blood stream infection.

Critical illness leads to rapid colonization of the oropharynx with pathogenic bacteria, caused by changes in the host defense, antibiotic exposure, and possible changes in bacterial adhesion and host surface receptors.
Many of the usual host defense mechanisms including immune function are less effective.
Profound changes occur in the function and structure of the alveoli.
Neutrophil dysfunction and inadequate phagocytosis increase susceptibility to infection.

Use an infection control bundle to prevent VAP. Specific interventions are discussed below. One such bundle for post-operative patients is I COUGH, for incentive spirometry, coughing and deep breathing, oral care, understanding (education), getting out of bed, and head of bed elevation. B
Inhaled aminoglycosides are also effective. B
Use a new ventilator circuit for each patient, and change it when soiled or damaged. Also use a heat and moisture exchanger and change every 5 to 7 days. B
Perform continuous suction of subglottic secretions when intubation is expected to last more than 72 hours. B
Toothbrushing daily has been shown in a meta-analysis to reduce the likelihood of HAP (NNT=12), especially in patients who were mechanically ventilated.B

Preventive strategies that are not recommended or for which there is insufficient evidence to routinely recommend include white cell stimulating factors, chest PT, bacterial filters, kinetic or continuous lateral rotational therapy beds, prophylactic antibiotics, or IV immunoglobulin. B

Use an infection control bundle to prevent VAP. One such bundle for post-operative patients is I COUGH, for incentive spirometry, coughing and deep breathing, oral care, understanding (education), getting out of bed, and head of bed elevation. While infection control bundles do appear to help, it is unclear what specific components lead to reduction in VAP.

A Swiss trial evaluated a 5 item bundle (oral care, dysphagia screening and management, mobilisation, discontinuation of non-indicated proton-pump inhibitors, and respiratory therapy) in 9 medical and surgical department over baseline (14-33 months), implementation (2 months) and intervention (3-22 months) periods. They found a reduction in the incidence of non-ventilator hospital acquired pneumonia (0.90 vs 1.42 episodes/1000 patient-days, incidence ratio 0.69, p = 0.008).
A Cochrane review found no evidence that incentive spirometry in post-op patients prevented respiratory complications.

Perform oral decontamination with chlorhexidine or povidone iodine. However, early administration of oral chlorhexidine (before 12 hours) in intubated patients was not associated with a reduction in VAP and can increase mortality.

A meta-analysis identified 15 studies with 2786 patients comparing daily toothbrushing with care as usual. Toothbrushing led to a significantly lower incidence of HAP (RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.56 - 0.81; I2=0%, NNT = 12). This was especially true for the patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (RR 0.68; 0.57 - 0.82; I2=0). Toothbrushing was also associated with less time to extubation (mean difference [MD] -1.24 days; -2.42 to -0.06 days) and shorter ICU length of stay (MD -1.78 days; -2.85 to -0.70 days). Finally, patients who received toothbrushing had decreased ICU mortality (RR 0.81; 0.69-0.95; I2=0); however, this finding did not hold up in a sensitivity analysis that only included the studies at low risk of bias.
Use a new ventilator circuit for each patient, and change it when soiled or damaged. Also use a heat and moisture exchanger and change every 5 to 7 days.
Perform continuous suction of subglottic secretions when intubation is expected to last more than 72 hours. Elevate the head of the bed to 30° to 45° for patients who are at high risk of VAP.

Preventive strategies that are not recommended or for which there is insufficient evidence to routinely recommend include white cell stimulating factors, chest PT, bacterial filters, kinetic or continuous lateral rotational therapy beds, prophylactic antibiotics, or IV immunoglobulin. A tapered-cuff endotracheal tube does not reduce the risk of VAP compared with use of a spherical-cuff ET tube.

There is some evidence that the use of a continuous endotracheal cuff pressure control system and/or an endotracheal tube with a lumen for subglottic secretion damage could help to prevent VAP in patients requiring more than 48 hours of mechanical ventilation.

Stress ulcer prophylaxis is commonly recommended for mechanically ventilated pateints. However, its use has been associated with C. difficile infection and VAP. A small pilot trial and systematic review found no evidence that its use either reduces GI bleeding or affects mortality or infection rates.

A randomized trial in 198 patients with return of spontaneous circulation following out of hospital cardiac arrest who were receiving targeted temperature management, adding 2 days of IV amoxiclav 1000 mg/200 mg three times daily significantly reduced the incidence of ventilator associated pneumonia (17% vs 34%, p = 0.03, NNT = 6).

A French trial randomized 850 patients who had been mechanically ventilated for at least 72 hours to inhaled amikacin or placebo once daily. Patients in the amikacin group had a lower incidence of a first episode of ventilator-associated pneumonia per 1000 days of invasive mechanical ventilation (16 vs 23; rate ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.49 - 0.94). Infection-related ventilator-associated complications were also decreased in the amikacin group (18% vs 26%; hazard ratio 0.66; 0.50 - 0.89).

A systematic review identified 7 RCTs with 1445 patients comparing inhaled antibiotics vs placebo or usual care in patients on a mechanical ventilator. Inhaled antibiotics reduced the risk of VAP (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53-0.89) but not mortality or length of stay. Inhaled aminoglycosides appeared to be most effective.
Multiplex PCR can be a useful tool in appropriate selection of antibiotic prophylaxis in patients with suspected VAP or HAP.
A small RCT of 120 patients demonstrated evidence that higher airway pressure levels with mechanical ventilation may reduce the risk of VAP.
A trial randomized 5982 mechanically ventilated patients to selective decontamination of the digestive tract (SDD) or usual care. There was no difference in any primary or secondary outcomes.
However, a systematic review of 32 RCTs with 24,389 participants comparing SDD with usual care found a small reduction in mortality with SDD (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.82-0.99, I2 = 34%).
A randomized trial with 2650 ventilated patients compared the probiotic L rhamnosus GG with placebo. There was no reduction in the likelihood of patients developing VAP.
A randomized trial with 213 participants found no reduction in the likelihood of VAP among those given the monoclonal antibody suvratoxumab which targets the Staph aureus alpha toxin.
A randomized trial with 434 patients compared continuous regulation of tracheal cuff pressure with manual adjustment 3 times daily (usual care) and found no effect on outcomes.
Suspect VAP in any patient with new lung infiltrate on chest radiography and one or more of the following symptoms: fever >38°C, leukocytosis, and purulent tracheal secretions. B
Order blood cultures and pleural fluid culture (if effusion) as well as chest radiography. C
Send semi-quantitative lower respiratory tract cultures, using endotrachial aspiration in patients with suspected VAP.C
In patients with suspected HAP obtain non-invasive microbiologic studies (spontaneous expectoration, sputum induction, or nasotracheal suctioning in non-ventilated patients). C
Use the clinical pulmonary infection score (CPIS) to help with diagnosis of VAP. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Culture negative, positive CT angiogram, or VQ scan
Culture negative, smoking history, progressive symptoms
Disease onset in fifth to six decade of life, responds well to steroids
Recent use of offending med (e.g. amiodarone)
Culture could be negative, + fungitell assay, no improvement on antibiotics

list.listitem: Patients with VAP typically may present with fever, purulent tracheobronchial secretions, and impaired oxygenation. Suspect VAP in any patient with new lung infiltrate on chest radiography plus at least one of the following: fever >38°C, leukocytosis, and purulent tracheal secretions. Increasing numbers of clinical symptoms increase specificity but decrease sensitivity.

The following patients are at risk for multidrug resistant pathogens: those with recent antimicrobial therapy, a current hospitalization of 5 days or longer, in a community with a high rate of antibiotic resistance, coming from nursing home, on infusion therapy or dialysis, or home wound care.

Leukocytosis or leukopenia may be seen in patients with VAP. When VAP is clinically suspected, order CXR to look for new or progressive infiltrate, and assess oxygenation. Also order blood cultures.Lung ultrasound in 99 patients with suspected VAP was moderately acurate (sensitivity and specificity ~80%).

The 2016 IDSA/American Thoracic Society guidelines recommend obtaining a non-invasive sample via endotrachial aspiration with semiquantitative culture results over more invasive methods. If an invasive approach with bronchoscopy is chosen, antibiotics should be withheld if the culture results are below the diagnostic threshold for VAP.

In patients with suspected HAP, obtain non-invasive microbiologic studies. Techniques for non-invasive specimen collection include spontaneous expectoration, sputum induction, or nasotracheal suctioning. In patients who have HAP but subsequently are intubated, obtain the specimen using endotracheal aspiration.
Patients with a large pleural effusion should have diagnostic thoracentesis to rule out empyema.

Serum procalcitonin, soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells (sTREM-1), and c-reactive protein are not recommended to guide the decision to prescribe antibiotics in patients with HAP or VAP.

In patients with suspected HAP or VAP, the modified Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score criteria are not recommended as a supplement to clinical criteria when deciding whether or not to initiate antibiotics.

In patients with clinically suspected VAP, the detection of alpha-amylase in bronchioalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid is associated with an increased likelihood of pneumonia and is also associated with risk factors for aspiration.

A meta-analysis found that pentraxin 3 protein testing in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid is a moderately accurate test for the diagnosis of ventilator-associated pneumonia (77% sensitive, 80% specific) but there was considerable heterogeneity among the included studies; the largest study found the lowest sensitivity (69%). The cost is significantly greater than c-reactive protein and it has no clear advantage.

Multiple cross displacement amplification is a promising rapid test for the many strains of P. aeruginosa has a high sensitivity and specificity and is arguably cost effective, but needs further research to establish clinical significance.
Suspect VAP in patients with fever, purulent tracheobronchial secretions, leukocytosis, and decline in oxygenation with radiographic infiltrate that is new or progressing.

Obtain lower respiratory tract samples using endotracheal aspiratio for microscopy and semi-quantitative culture, and blood cultures. Perform thoracocentesis for non-loculated pleural effusion of >10 mm in diameter on lateral decubitus chest radiograph.

Antibiotic selection in patients with HAP or VAP should be based on culture results preferably, rather than empiric selection. Patients with negative culture (<10,000 cfu/ml) should have antibiotics withheld. Reassess at 48 to 72 hours. If clinical improvement and cultures negative, consider stopping antibiotics; if cultures positive, try to de-escalate antibiotics, and reassess at 7 to 8 days. If no clinical improvement, consider other pathogens and if culture positive adjust antibiotics.
Select antimicrobial therapy based on the absence or presence of risk factors for MDR pathogens.C
Choice of antibiotic should be dictated by local microbiology, cost, availability, and formulary restriction.B
Combination therapy should be used if the patients likely to be infected with MDR pathogen and/or patients at high risk of mortality. B
If the patient receives initial appropriate antibiotic therapy, a 7 day course is recommended provided the patient has a good clinical response. A

Early appropriate broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy should be prescribed with adequate dosing to optimize antimicrobial efficacy. For patients with no known risk factors for multidrug resistant pathogens, initial recommended antibiotics should cover staph aureus, pseudomonas aeruginosa, and other gram negative bacilli. The selection of an antibiotic should be guided by the results of noninvasive sampling (endotrachial aspiration) with semiquantitative culture. Local hospitals should generate antibiograms that should guide antibiotic selection for patients with HAP or VAP based on local resistance and susceptibility patterns.

Risk factors for multidrug resistant pathogens in patients with HAP or VAP: prolonged hospitalization (>5 days), admission from a nursing home or extended care facility, ARDS preceding VAP, acute renal replacement therapy,or IV antibiotic therapy in the past 3 months.

Recommendations from the Infectious DIsease Society of America/American Thoracic Society guidelines for specific patient subgroups with HAP or VAP are summarized below (see Table 1 for dosing of each antibiotic): VAP where empiric MRSA coverage and double anti-pseudomonal/gram negative coverage are recommended (patient has risk factors or >10-20% of staph isolates are methicillin resesistant or resistance is unknown): (1) Vancomycin or linezolid, plus (2) piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime or ceftazidime or imipenem or meropenem or aztreonam, plus (3) ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, an aminoglycoside, colistin, or polymyxin. VAP when empiric treatment for MRSA is not required: prescribe piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, levofloxacin, imipenem or meropenem. If treatment for MSSA is required, use oxacillin, nafcillin or cefazolin. HAP in patients not at high risk of mortality and no factors increasing risk for MRSA: Single antibiotic therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 gm IV q 6 hrs, cefepime 2 gm IV q 8 hrs, or levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily. HAP in patients not at high risk of mortality but with factors increasing the likelihood of MRSA: Dual antibiotic therapy, with vancomycin or linezolidone plus one of the following: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, imipenem, meropenem, or aztreonam. HAP in patients at high risk of mortality or IV antibiotics in previous 3 months: Triple antibiotic therapy with vancomycin or linezolid plus two of the following (avoid prescribing 2 beta-lactams): piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, imipenem, meropenem, aztreonam, amikacin, gentamicin, or tobramycin.

De-escalation of antibiotic therapy is recommended: this is defined as choosing antibiotics targetted more closely to culture results when available for patients with HAP or VAP, and should be considered once data on the results of lower respiratory tract culture available and patient clinical response after 48 to 72 hours is assessed. The recommended duration of therapy for most patients with HAP or VAP is 7 days. Procalcitonin plus clinical criteria can be used to determine when antibiotics can be discontinued in patients with HAP or VAP.

Patients with HAP or VAP due to acinetobacter species should be treated with either carbapenem or ampicillin/sulbactam is susceptible. If only sensitive to polymyxin, adjunctive inhaled colistin is recommended.
Patients should be treated for potentially resistant organism regardless of when during hospitalization develop pneumonia.
The DRIP score can predict the likelihood of resistant organisms in a patient hospitalized with pneumonia.
Avoid aminoglycosides or colistin in patients with HAP or VAP if alternative agents with adequate Gram-negative coverage are available.

A systematic review compared 7 to 8 days with 10 to 15 days of antibiotics for patients with VAP. Outcomes were better for the shorter duration of therapy, with less recurrences due to multi-drug resistant organisms. The exception was for non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli (i.e. pseudomonas or acinetobacter), where longer duration therapy was preferred.

For patients with MRSA pneumonia, vancomycin is standard therapy. It is important to dose to achieve at least 15 mg/L trough concentration. Linezolid has been shown to be similarly effective to vancomycin for MRSA hospital acquired pneumonia in two RCTs. Combining the results of these studies found a possible benefit to linezolid over vancomycin for these patients (clinical cure rate 59% vs 35%, p <0.01).

A randomized trial of 133 post-operative patients with HAP or VAP found that nebulized amikacin resulted in better clinical cure rates, less time in the ICU, and less impact on kidney function than IV amikacin. However, a second trial that added nebulized amikacin /fosfomycin to standard therapy for gram negative VAP found no clinical benefits in 143 patients. A systematic review identified 11 studies, mostly small, of nebulized antibiotic therapies in patients with VAP. They found some evidence that it may reduce nephrotoxicity, but also heterogeneous evidence that it may be associated with a higher risk of respiratory complications.

A trial randomized 181 patients with acinetobacter baumannii-calcoaceticus complex pneumonia (mostly hospital and ventilator acquired) to sulbactam-durlobactam (1 gm of each drug every 6 hrs) or colistin (2.5 mg/kg over 30 minutes every 12 h) for 7 to 14 days. The 28-day all-cause mortality was lower in the sulbactam-durlobactam group (19% vs 32%, mean difference -13.2%, 95% CI -30% to 3.5%. While not superior it was non-inferior. Nephrotoxicity was lower with sulbacta-durlobactam (13% vs 38%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).
Antibiotics are not recommended for patients with ventilator-associated tracheobronchitis.
Educate healthcare personnel about local epidemiology, risk factors, and evidence-based preventive measures.
High frequency oscillation does not improve outcomes in adults with ARDS.
No difference in long-term outcomes with full vs trophic feeding for acute lung injury patients.

As compared with a usual level of mobilization, a randomized trial with 750 patients found that increasing early mobilization for mechanically ventilated patients in the ICU does not increase the number of days alive and out of the hospital and may increase adverse events.
In patients with VAP, the presence of bacteremia, a higher APACHE score, a compromised immune system, and older age are independent risk factors for mortality. B

The presence of the following factors: multi-lobar involvement on chest radiography, a Simplified Acute Pathophysiology Score (SAPS) II score greater than 37, platelet count less than 150,000, delayed or inappropriate antimicrobial therapy, severity of illness, and infection with a resistant organism (pseudomonas, sternotrophomonas, acinetobacter spp.) are associated with higher mortality rate in patients with VAP.
Based on a meta-analysis of patient data from randomized trials of VAP, the attributable mortality of VAP was an estimated 13%.
Serial assessment of clinical response to initial empiric therapy is important to assess the need for changing therapy as well as de-escalation of therapy according culture results. B
